case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Secretary of Homeland Security's decision to revoke an approved immigrant visa petition under 8 U.S.C. 1155 is subject to judicial review in federal district court, or whether such review is barred by the jurisdiction-stripping provision at 8 U.S.C. 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii).
case_analysis.legal_provision: 8 U.S.C. 1155 (visa petition revocation statute, granting the Secretary authority to revoke any approved immigrant visa petition 'at any time, for what he deems to be good and sufficient cause') in conjunction with 8 U.S.C. 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) (jurisdiction-stripping provision barring judicial review of 'any other decision or action' by the Secretary 'the authority for which is specified' to be in his 'discretion' under Title II of the INA).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner Amina Bouarfa argues that the revocation of her husband's approved immigrant visa petition should be subject to judicial review because: (1) the jurisdiction-stripping provision of 8 U.S.C. 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) does not bar review of all discretionary decisions, but only those where Congress has explicitly and specifically committed the decision to agency discretion; (2) 8 U.S.C. 1155 does not sufficiently specify that revocation is a purely discretionary act immune from all judicial scrutiny; (3) permitting unreviewable revocations would eliminate meaningful legal recourse for petitioners whose approved visa petitions are arbitrarily or erroneously revoked; and (4) longstanding principles of administrative law, including the presumption of judicial review of agency action under the APA, counsel against interpreting ambiguous statutory language to foreclose all judicial oversight of potentially erroneous government action.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents Secretary Mayorkas and the Department of Homeland Security argue that: (1) the plain text of 8 U.S.C. 1155 expressly commits revocation authority to the Secretary's discretion, thereby triggering the jurisdiction-stripping bar of 8 U.S.C. 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii); (2) Congress deliberately used broad, discretion-conferring language in 1155 ('for what he deems to be good and sufficient cause'), signaling clear legislative intent to insulate such decisions from judicial review; (3) the Eleventh Circuit correctly held that district courts lack jurisdiction to review visa petition revocations; and (4) the Secretary's broad statutory authority over admission of noncitizens, combined with the explicit jurisdiction-stripping language, forecloses district court review as a matter of statutory interpretation.

Kucana v. Holder, 558 U.S. 233 (2010) - interpreting 8 U.S.C. 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) and distinguishing between discretion specified by statute versus discretion conferred by regulation

INS v. St. Cyr, 533 U.S. 289 (2001) - articulating strong presumption in favor of judicial review of immigration decisions
Guerrero-Lasprilla v. Barr, 589 U.S. 221 (2020) - addressing scope of judicial review limitations in immigration statutes
APA Section 701(a)(2), 5 U.S.C. 701(a)(2) - precluding judicial review of agency action committed to agency discretion by law
Chevron U.S.A. Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council, 467 U.S. 837 (1984) - deference to agency interpretation of ambiguous statutes
Traynor v. Turnage, 485 U.S. 535 (1988) - addressing scope of jurisdiction-stripping statutes
Webster v. Doe, 486 U.S. 592 (1988) - addressing limits of unreviewable agency discretion under APA

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor raises the most serious challenge by invoking the 'clear and convincing evidence' standard from Kucana and the human stakes for immigrant families, but I find that the tripartite textual markers in Section 1155 — 'may,' 'at any time,' and 'what he deems to be good and sufficient cause' — collectively satisfy that demanding standard. The Kucana distinction between statutory and regulatory discretion, which Justice Kagan articulates with particular clarity, is dispositive here: Congress itself wrote the discretionary standard into the statute, not an agency regulation, placing this squarely within 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii)'s bar. Consistent with my minimalist approach, I would write narrowly to hold only that district courts lack jurisdiction over these revocation decisions while expressly leaving open whether constitutional avenues of review remain available — a limiting principle that addresses Justice Sotomayor's concern about wholly unreviewable arbitrary action without expanding the holding beyond what the text requires. The institutional legitimacy of this Court is best served by faithfully applying the statutory text Congress enacted rather than stretching jurisdictional grants to reach outcomes we might prefer on policy grounds.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor's conversion is telling — even the Justice most sympathetic to petitioners has recognized that Kucana's own internal logic defeats the petitioner's position here, because Kucana's presumption favoring review was explicitly premised on the distinction between agency-conferred and congressionally-specified discretion, and Section 1155 falls unambiguously on the statutory side of that line. Justice Kagan's point about the absence of judicially manageable standards reinforces my textualist analysis: 'for what he deems to be good and sufficient cause' makes the Secretary's subjective judgment the operative legal standard, leaving courts without any external benchmark — precisely the condition that renders review not merely disfavored but structurally impossible. My confidence increases slightly from 0.78 to 0.85 because the convergence of colleagues across ideological lines on the Kucana statutory/regulatory distinction confirms that this is not a close textual question, and I remain persuaded that the tripartite discretion-conferring language in Section 1155 constitutes the clear and convincing evidence St. Cyr demands before reading a statute to foreclose review. I would add, consistent with my originalist methodology, that the Founders understood executive discretion in matters of alien admission and exclusion to be particularly broad, which provides additional historical grounding for reading Section 1155 as Congress intended.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: After reviewing my colleagues' arguments across two rounds of deliberation, I am more confident than ever in the Respondent's position. Justice Kagan's analysis of the Kucana distinction is dispositive for my textualist methodology: the critical line Kucana drew was between agency-conferred discretion (reviewable) and congressionally-specified discretion (unreviewable under § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii)), and § 1155's tripartite language — 'may,' 'at any time,' 'for what he deems to be good and sufficient cause' — places this squarely on the statutory side of that line. Justice Sotomayor's concern about wholly unreviewable arbitrary action is not without force, and I share Chief Justice Roberts's instinct to leave open constitutional avenues of review for truly egregious cases, but that concern cannot override Congress's deliberate textual choice — my role is to apply the law as written, not to rewrite it based on equitable sympathies, however genuine. The absence of any judicially manageable standard against which to measure 'good and sufficient cause,' as Justice Kagan and Heckler v. Chaney together confirm, means courts would be substituting their own subjective judgment for the Secretary's, which is precisely what Congress foreclosed.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: After two rounds of deliberation, I remain persuaded by Justice Kagan's core analytical move: Kucana's presumption favoring judicial review was specifically premised on the concern that agencies shouldn't be able to silently strip jurisdiction through their own regulations, but when Congress itself writes 'for what he deems to be good and sufficient cause' directly into the statute, it has provided the clear and convincing evidence that Kucana and St. Cyr demand. My deepest concern — that petitioners like Ms. Bouarfa are left without any meaningful check on arbitrary government action — is real and I do not minimize it, but Justice Roberts' limiting principle preserving constitutional avenues of review partially addresses that concern, and as Justice Jackson acknowledges despite sharing my commitment to protecting vulnerable populations, the Kucana distinction between statutory and regulatory discretion is the operative line and Section 1155 falls unambiguously on the statutory side. I write separately to emphasize that this outcome is a policy failure Congress must remedy: immigrant families deserve a meaningful opportunity to challenge revocations that can destroy their lives, and the absence of judicially manageable standards reflects a legislative gap that Congress — not this Court — must fill. I maintain my reluctant concurrence with the Respondent's position while urging Congress to restore oversight mechanisms that honor both the rule of law and basic human dignity.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor raises the most serious challenge to my position by invoking the 'clear and convincing evidence' standard from Kucana and the human stakes for petitioners like Bouarfa, but I find that the tripartite textual markers in § 1155 — 'may,' 'at any time,' and 'what he deems' — collectively satisfy even that demanding standard. The phrase 'what he deems to be good and sufficient cause' is not merely discretion-conferring in a general sense; it makes the Secretary's own subjective judgment the operative legal standard, which means there is no external benchmark against which a court could measure the decision — precisely the condition Heckler v. Justice Jackson's point about Congress itself embedding the discretionary language directly in the statute, as distinguished from the regulatory discretion at issue in Kucana, is the critical analytical move here: Kucana's presumption-favoring-review logic was premised on the idea that agency-conferred discretion shouldn't silently strip jurisdiction, but when Congress writes 'deems' into the statute itself, it has spoken with the clarity Kucana demanded. I remain persuaded that the workability concern and the textual clarity together rebut the presumption, though I would leave open constitutional avenues of review as Justice Roberts suggests.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: After reviewing the full conference, I find the convergence of my colleagues across methodological lines — from Justice Sotomayor's reluctant concession to Justice Kagan's workability analysis — actually reinforces rather than merely reflects the textual case. The argument that most tested my position was Justice Sotomayor's invocation of St. Cyr's 'clear and convincing evidence' standard, but as I noted in my prior reasoning, that standard is satisfied here by Congress's own deliberate word choice embedding 'what he deems' directly into Section 1155 — this is not a case of agency self-delegation of unreviewability, which was Kucana's core concern. Justice Kagan's point about the absence of judicially manageable standards is particularly compelling from a textualist standpoint: when Congress writes 'deems to be good and sufficient cause,' it has not merely conferred discretion but has made the Secretary's subjective judgment the operative legal standard itself, leaving courts without any external benchmark — a structural signal that Congress intended finality here. I write separately to emphasize that constitutional avenues of review remain open and that my holding is narrow: we decide only that Article III courts lack statutory jurisdiction over these revocation decisions, not that the Constitution is indifferent to arbitrary or discriminatory revocations.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: After two rounds of deliberation, I find the convergence of analysis across the Court's ideological spectrum — from Justice Sotomayor's reluctant concession to Justice Thomas's textualist analysis — reinforces rather than undermines my position. Justice Kagan's point about the absence of judicially manageable standards remains the most practically compelling element of the analysis: 'what he deems to be good and sufficient cause' makes the Secretary's subjective judgment the operative standard, leaving courts without any external benchmark, which is precisely the condition that makes judicial review unworkable rather than merely inconvenient. I maintain my view that constitutional avenues of review — due process, equal protection — remain available for truly egregious cases, which addresses the equity concerns without distorting the statutory text Congress enacted.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor's conversion is itself instructive — she correctly identifies that Kucana's own internal logic, properly understood, cuts against the petitioner's position because the Kucana Court drew its presumption-favoring-review principle specifically in the context of agency-conferred discretion, not congressionally-specified discretion. The fact that Justice Jackson, who brings genuine concern for individuals facing unreviewable government action, nonetheless arrives at the Respondent's position through careful textual analysis confirms that this is not a case where ideological priors are driving outcomes but rather one where the statutory text compels a particular result. I remain persuaded that the tripartite markers in § 1155 — 'may,' 'at any time,' and 'what he deems to be good and sufficient cause' — constitute the clear and convincing evidence Kucana demands, and Justice Kagan's point about the absence of judicially manageable standards reinforces that Congress made a deliberate structural choice to vest this judgment in the Secretary's unreviewable discretion. I would write to preserve constitutional avenues of review as Justice Roberts suggests, ensuring our holding is narrow and does not foreclose due process challenges to truly arbitrary or constitutionally infirm revocations.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Barrett's textualist argument remains the strongest challenge to my position — she correctly identifies that Section 1155's 'he deems' language is statutory rather than regulatory, satisfying Kucana's precise condition, and that the phrase may encompass the entire decisional process including factual predicates. However, after reviewing the full conference, I am persuaded that Justice Kagan's structural argument is correct on the critical point: the jurisdiction-stripping bar in 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) targets the exercise of discretion, not the non-discretionary legal and factual predicates that condition whether discretion may lawfully be exercised at all. The anomaly Justice Kagan identifies — that initial petition denials on identical grounds remain reviewable while revocations would not — is textually incoherent and reinforces that Congress did not speak with the unmistakable clarity INS v. St. Cyr demands before we conclude it foreclosed all review of predicate determinations. As Chief Justice, I would assign the majority opinion with instructions to write narrowly — holding only that courts retain jurisdiction to review non-discretionary legal and factual predicates to the revocation decision, without opining on the merits of the Secretary's ultimate discretionary judgment — a formulation that should hold our six-justice coalition together while preserving institutional legitimacy and leaving room for Justice Jackson's more cautious concurrence.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch press the predicate-discretion distinction with considerable force, but I remain unpersuaded because it lacks textual foundation in Section 1155 itself. Unlike statutory schemes where Congress separately specifies objective criteria for a threshold finding and then grants discretion over the ultimate disposition — thereby creating a textually discernible two-step structure — Section 1155 contains no such bifurcation: the phrase 'for what he deems to be good and sufficient cause' commits the entire determination, including the factual assessment of whether cause exists, to the Secretary's judgment in a single, undivided grant. Justice Barrett correctly identifies that the absence of objective statutory criteria in Section 1155 distinguishes it from initial petition adjudications, and this structural difference is precisely why the 'he deems' language represents a deliberate congressional choice to subsume the factual predicate within the discretionary grant rather than leaving it separately reviewable. Justice Roberts's constitutional avoidance argument from Webster v. Doe deserves respect, but the constitutional question here — whether due process requires judicial review of a discretionary immigration benefit revocation — is not sufficiently grave or clearly presented to override the plain statutory text, particularly when petitioners retain mandamus for ministerial violations and other procedural protections. The strong presumption of reviewability articulated in St. Cyr and Kucana must yield when Congress has spoken with the clarity that 'he deems' provides, and I would hold that Section 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) bars judicial review of the revocation decision in its entirety.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan's predicate-determination argument is the most sophisticated challenge to my position, and I have genuinely wrestled with it — but I remain unpersuaded for a reason none of my colleagues have adequately answered: Section 1155 contains no objective statutory criteria for what constitutes 'good and sufficient cause,' which is precisely what distinguishes it from the initial petition context where Congress specified substantive eligibility requirements. When Congress establishes no external criteria against which to measure the agency's factual finding, there is no analytically coherent way to separate the 'predicate factual determination' from the 'discretionary judgment' — the 'he deems' language is Congress's deliberate choice to commit the entire inquiry, including the factual assessment, to the Secretary's unreviewable judgment. Justice Barrett makes this point most clearly, and it is textually decisive: the predicate-versus-discretion distinction only works when Congress has specified criteria that render the predicate finding objectively verifiable, which it has not done here. The structural anomaly Justice Kagan identifies regarding initial denials is real but does not override the plain text, because initial petition adjudications are governed by separate statutory provisions with specified criteria — the asymmetry reflects congressional design, not incoherence.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Barrett's textualist argument remains the most formidable challenge to my position — she correctly identifies that Section 1155's 'he deems' language is statutory rather than regulatory, satisfying Kucana's precise condition, and that the phrase encompasses the entire decisional process without textually carving out factual predicates. But I find this reading ultimately untenable because it proves too much: as Justice Kagan articulates, the non-discretionary determination of whether a marriage is fraudulent is a legal obligation the agency must discharge correctly before any discretion attaches, and Congress cannot be understood to have silently stripped review of such predicate findings through language that speaks only to the ultimate discretionary call. The structural anomaly Justice Kavanaugh highlights — that initial petition denials on identical grounds remain reviewable while revocations would not — reinforces that Congress did not intend the jurisdictional bar to swallow threshold factual determinations, and the constitutional avoidance canon under St. Cyr and Zadvydas demands unmistakably clear congressional direction before we leave families like the Bouarfas with zero recourse against agency factual error. I write separately to emphasize that this holding must be understood through the lens of real human consequences: unreviewable agency error in the family-based immigration context produces irreversible family separation, and the rule of law requires at minimum that courts can ask whether the agency correctly determined the predicate facts that triggered its authority.
